History:
- Presenting complaint: New-onset severe headache began yesterday (mid-morning).
- Location/timing/quality: Left-sided posterior (occipital) head pain, throbbing, built up gradually over a short period.
- Severity/progression: Pain rated ~8/10; not relieved by an analgesic dose taken yesterday (Nurofen/ibuprofen); persistent through the day and interfering with ability to work.
- Associated symptoms: Denies nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, visual disturbance, tingling, numbness, weakness, fever, rash, or neck stiffness. No change with posture, coughing, sneezing, bending. Slept through the night.
- Triggers/preceding events: Patient reports no recent trauma, no new stressors or lifestyle changes identified. Family history notable for mother with migraines and hypertension.
- Context: First significant headache for patient.

Past Medical History:
- Chronic illnesses: None reported.
- Medications: Took Nurofen (ibuprofen) yesterday — dose/route/frequency not documented. No regular prescription medications reported.
- Allergies: None reported.
- Surgical/hospitalization history: Not recorded.
- Family history: Mother with hypertension and migraines.
- Social history: Lives with partner; occupation: designer. Denies tobacco, alcohol, and recreational drug use. Pregnancy status not documented.

Physical Examination:
- General/observations: Patient conversational and alert during consultation.
- Vital signs: Not recorded.
- Head/neck: No throat swelling reported. No rash observed/reported.
- Neurologic/visual: No visual disturbance reported; no weakness, numbness, or sensory changes reported.
- Meningeal signs: No neck stiffness reported.
- Relevant negatives (reported by patient): No fever, no vomiting, no photophobia/aural symptoms.
- Formal physical exam findings: Not recorded.

Impression:
- One-line clinical impression: New-onset severe left occipital throbbing headache, most consistent with a primary headache disorder (probable migraine) given unilateral throbbing quality, severity, and family history.
- DDx (consistent with transcript):
  - Migraine — high likelihood: unilateral throbbing occipital pain, severe (8/10), family history of migraine.
  - Cervicogenic headache / tension-type — medium likelihood: posterior unilateral location could reflect cervical or tension-type origin though neck pain/movement triggers not reported.
  - Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) — low likelihood: new severe headache warrants consideration, but lack of sudden thunderclap onset, vomiting, neck stiffness, focal deficits, or loss of consciousness argues against typical SAH.

Management Plan:
- Immediate/advised measures:
  - Start a stronger analgesic as recommended by clinician (alternative to ibuprofen) — specific medication name and dose not documented; clinician indicated a prescription will be provided from the pharmacy.
  - Take analgesic regularly with food as advised.
  - Paracetamol may be taken in combination with the prescribed analgesic (per clinician).
  - Rest and ensure good hydration.
- Safety-net / red flags and when to seek urgent care:
  - Advise patient to seek immediate care or contact clinician if pain worsens or if any new symptoms develop: fever, rash, vomiting, neck stiffness, focal neurological deficits, or other concerning features.
- Follow-up:
  - If headache does not settle within 1–2 days after starting the prescribed medication, contact clinic for re-evaluation and planning of further management.
  - Clinician will reassess and determine need for further investigations or specialist referral if symptoms persist or new features emerge.

Patient Summary:
- 28-year-old female with sudden-onset (yesterday mid-morning) severe left occipital throbbing headache (8/10), first such episode, not relieved by a single dose of ibuprofen. Clinician advised a stronger analgesic (prescription to be issued), paracetamol, rest, and hydration, with instructions to return if worse or not improved within 1–2 days.

Key Takeaways:
- Take the prescribed stronger pain relief regularly with food; paracetamol may be used as instructed.
- Rest and maintain hydration.
- Return immediately or call if red-flag symptoms develop (fever, rash, vomiting, neck stiffness, focal weakness) or if no improvement in 1–2 days.

Next Steps:
- Patient to start prescribed analgesic (prescription to be provided from pharmacy; medication name/dose not documented).
- Re-evaluation planned if symptoms worsen or fail to improve within 48 hours; further investigations or referral will be arranged as clinically indicated at that time.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs (BP, pulse, temperature), focused neurologic and head/neck physical exam findings, pregnancy status, detailed medication dose/route/frequency for the recommended prescription, prior headache history details (e.g., lifetime migraine history), and any allergy reconciliation documentation.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted — DDx is consistent with transcript.
- Transcript quality: Clear and audible; consultation content adequate for an initial remote assessment though objective examination and vital signs are absent.
